claims.text: The lightweight high-entropy alloy initially has a nominally single-phase matrix.
The alloy initially has a homogeneous elemental distribution.
High configurational or mixing entropy stabilizes the alloy's single-phase matrix.
The single-phase matrix remains stabilized after lighter-element substitutions.
Selective elemental substitution maintains the alloy's low density.
Controlled thermal treatment promotes in situ formation of finely dispersed nanoscale oxide precipitates.
Nanoscale oxide precipitates hinder dislocation motion.
Hindering dislocation motion with nanoscale oxide precipitates increases mechanical strength.
Nanoscale oxide precipitates act as barriers against environmental attack.
Nanoscale oxide precipitates improve corrosion resistance.
Nanoscale oxide precipitates improve high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Relative to the untreated baseline, the thermally treated alloy should have significantly higher mechanical strength.
Relative to the untreated baseline, the thermally treated alloy should have a lower corrosion rate.
Relative to the untreated baseline, the thermally treated alloy should oxidize more slowly at high temperature.
Thermal treatment that produces nanoscale oxides should not materially compromise the alloy's low density.
Excessive thermal-processing temperature can coarsen the nanoscale oxide precipitates.
Excessive thermal-processing temperature can trigger multiphase decomposition.
Oxide coarsening or multiphase decomposition causes the predicted property benefits to vanish.
Composition changes that disrupt entropy stabilization can produce unwanted phase separation.
Comparable property improvements in the absence of the intended nanoscale oxide dispersion would falsify the proposed oxide-mediated mechanism.
